planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in moist, acidic soil; Maxine was found growing wild near DeRidder, Louisiana, and selected for its naturally open, umbrella-shaped canopy and above-average fruit size.

directions: Maxine is a western mayhaw selection found growing wild near DeRidder, Louisiana, and named for the finder's wife; it was chosen for combining above-average fruit size with a naturally open, umbrella-shaped canopy that needs little corrective pruning. It blooms later than early selections such as Royal Star, which helps its flowers dodge Gulf South late frosts, and it carries good field resistance to fire blight, the disease that most often limits mayhaw orchards in the humid South. Like other mayhaws, it thrives on wet, poorly drained, acidic ground where few other fruiting trees perform well, and it sets a heavier crop when planted with a second mayhaw cultivar for cross-pollination.

common_name: Royal Star Mayhaw (Early-Blooming Thornless Purple-Red Mayhaw)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in moist, acidic soil; Royal Star blooms early, so pair it with another early-flowering mayhaw such as Spectacular for reliable cross-pollination.

directions: Royal Star is an early-blooming western mayhaw selection valued for its nearly thornless, upright branching, which makes mowing and harvesting beneath the canopy far easier than with thorny seedling mayhaws. Its fruit ripens to a deep red verging on purple, giving jelly and syrup an unusually dark, rich color compared with the brighter red of most mayhaw cultivars. Because it flowers early in the season, it needs another early-blooming mayhaw such as Spectacular planted nearby to ensure good cross-pollination and fruit set. Grow it, like other mayhaws, on moist to wet, acidic ground in full sun.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in moist, acidic soil; Spectacular blooms early and needs a second early-flowering mayhaw such as Royal Star nearby for pollination.

directions: Spectacular is an early-blooming western mayhaw selection bred for unusually large fruit, running up to about 0.85 inch across, noticeably bigger than wild-collected mayhaw. Because it blooms early, it requires a second early-flowering cultivar such as Royal Star planted nearby for reliable cross-pollination and a full crop. Give it the same wet, acidic, full-sun conditions favored by all mayhaws, since it is no more tolerant of dry, upland soil than its relatives.

common_name: Hope 13 Mayhaw (Large Dark Red Fire-Blight-Resistant Mayhaw)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in moist, acidic soil; Hope 13 was selected for very large fruit and good fire blight resistance.

directions: Hope 13 is a western mayhaw selection prized for very large, dark red fruit approaching an inch across, among the largest of the named mayhaw cultivars. It carries good resistance to fire blight, a bacterial disease that can quickly kill susceptible mayhaw wood during warm, humid springs. Plant it on the moist to wet, acidic soil mayhaw naturally prefers, and site a second cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and a dependable crop.

common_name: Double G Mayhaw (Heavy-Bearing Texas Star x Royal Star Hybrid Mayhaw)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in moist, acidic soil; Double G is a Texas Star x Royal Star cross that needs little corrective pruning to form its naturally open canopy.

directions: Double G is a cross between the Texas Star and Royal Star mayhaw selections, chosen for dark red fruit with distinctive strawberry-colored pulp and for combining heavy production with some of the best fire blight resistance of any named mayhaw. Like Maxine, it develops a naturally open, upside-down-umbrella canopy that needs little pruning to fruit well. It blooms relatively late, which helps it avoid spring frost damage, and Louisiana growers report some of the heaviest yields among named mayhaw selections from this cultivar. Grow it on wet to moist, acidic soil in full sun with a second cultivar nearby for pollination.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in moist, acidic soil; Surprise is one of longtime Louisiana breeder Billy Craft's named mayhaw selections.

directions: Surprise is a western mayhaw selection developed by longtime Louisiana mayhaw breeder Billy Craft, producing clusters of scarlet fruit that ripen in May. It is grown alongside other Craft selections such as Maxine and Double G as part of an ongoing effort to replace wild-collected mayhaw with named, more productive cultivars. Site it on wet to moist, acidic ground in full sun, and plant a second mayhaw cultivar nearby to ensure good cross-pollination.

common_name: Ben More Black Currant (Late-Flowering Large-Fruited Black Currant)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Ben More needs a real winter chill and is not a realistic choice for USDA zone 8-9 gardens.

directions: Ben More is a black currant from the Scottish Crop Research Institute's 'Ben' breeding series, selected for very late flowering that lets it dodge spring frosts and for unusually large fruit borne in heavy strings on a vigorous, strong-branched bush. Its mid-late ripening window follows earlier Ben-series cultivars such as Ben Sarek and Ben Lomond, so growers who plant several Ben currants can stretch out the picking season. Like other black currants, it needs a substantial winter chill to flower and fruit well, so it performs best in cold-winter regions and is not a realistic choice for the mild winters of USDA zone 8-9. Grow it in full sun on moist, fertile, well-drained soil, and prune out wood older than three years each dormant season to keep the bush productive.

common_name: Belaruskaja Black Currant (Floral-Flavored Sweet Black Currant)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Belaruskaja is self-fertile but, like other black currants, needs cold winters and is not well suited to zone 8-9.

directions: Belaruskaja is a black currant cultivar bred in Belarus, selected for berries with an unusually rich, floral aroma and enough sugar to be enjoyed fresh rather than only cooked. It shows good resistance to white pine blister rust, the disease that once led many U.S. states to restrict Ribes planting, making it a lower-risk choice where local rules require rust-resistant cultivars. The plant is self-fertile and ripens in mid- to late summer, but like other black currants it needs a substantial winter chill to set a full crop, so it is best suited to cold-winter gardens rather than the Gulf South. Plant in full sun on moist, fertile, well-drained soil, and renew the bush by removing the oldest canes each dormant season.

common_name: Early Sulphur Gooseberry (Historic Very-Early Yellow Dessert Gooseberry)

planting.note: Set dormant bare-root or container bushes in fall or very early spring in fertile, well-drained soil; Early Sulphur needs a real winter chill and is best suited to cold-winter gardens rather than zone 8-9.

directions: Early Sulphur is one of the oldest English dessert gooseberry cultivars still in commerce, possibly identical to the 'Yellow Lion of Ward' introduced in 1825, and it remains valued for ripening earlier than almost any other gooseberry. Its primrose-yellow, hairy berries are prized for excellent flavor, equally suited to fresh eating and jam, and the bush grows in a strong, upright habit. Because gooseberries need a real winter chill to perform well, Early Sulphur is best grown in cold-winter climates rather than the mild-winter Gulf South. Plant in full sun to light shade on fertile, well-drained soil, and prune to an open center each dormant season to improve airflow and reduce mildew.

common_name: Roaring Lion Gooseberry (Historic Red Dessert Gooseberry)

planting.note: Set dormant bare-root or container bushes in fall or very early spring in fertile, well-drained soil; Roaring Lion needs cold winters and is best suited to collectors in cooler zones rather than zone 8-9.

directions: Roaring Lion is a historic English gooseberry cultivar that was carried in the American Pomological Society's fruit catalog from 1873 to 1897, bearing medium-sized, smooth, light red, subacid berries good for pies and preserves. Older trial records note it can lack vigor and is somewhat prone to mildew compared with tougher modern cultivars, so it suits heirloom collectors more than large-scale production. Like other European gooseberries, it needs a substantial winter chill and struggles in the mild, humid winters of the Gulf South. Grow it in full sun to light shade on fertile, well-drained soil, pruned to an open habit for good airflow.

common_name: Broom Girl Gooseberry (Large Pale-Yellow Dessert Gooseberry)

planting.note: Set dormant bare-root or container bushes in fall or very early spring in fertile, well-drained soil; Broom Girl needs cold winters and is best suited to cooler zones rather than zone 8-9.

directions: Broom Girl is an older English gooseberry cultivar grown for its large, pale yellow dessert fruit, ripening in mid- to late June, later than early cultivars such as Early Sulphur. It belongs to Ribes uva-crispa var. reclinatum, the trailing-stemmed European gooseberry group prized for large-fruited dessert types. As with other European gooseberries, it needs cold winters to flower and crop reliably, making it a better fit for cold-winter regions than the mild Gulf South. Plant in full sun to light shade on fertile, well-drained soil, and prune annually to an open center to reduce mildew pressure.
